articles.title_orig: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly fire that tested Beijing’s grip on city
articles.title_zh: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly fire that tested Beijing’s grip on city
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG — Hong Kong ’s leader made a rare apology Thursday for a residential fire that killed 168 people last year, announcing that a top housing official would resign after an investigation blamed corruption and regulatory failures for the Chinese territory’s worst human-caused disaster in decades .
The Nov. 26, 2025, fire at Wang Fuk Court , a high-rise housing estate in the suburban district of Tai Po, swiftly engulfed seven of its eight towers, killing 110 women and 58 men ranging in age from 6 months to 98 years old. Thousands of others were displaced from their homes at the complex, which was undergoing major renovations at the time of the blaze.
The tragedy provoked widespread public grief and anger and was widely seen as the first major test for the Hong Kong government since Beijing imposed a sweeping national security law in 2020 in response to pro-democracy protests. Critics say the law, which Hong Kong and Chinese officials say was necessary to restore stability, has been used to stifle dissent in the former British colony.
Calls for accountability and transparency after the fire were quickly met with warnings from Hong Kong and Chinese officials, who said that “external hostile forces” were trying to re-create the chaos of the 2019 protests, which sometimes turned violent.
John Lee , Hong Kong’s top leader, said he was “deeply saddened” by the fire’s impact on the community.
“After self-reflection, I have considered that the government should roll out a large number of measures for reform, and a lot of work has to be carried out,” he said at a news conference.
“In my capacity as chief executive, I apologize to all the victims and members of the public,” said Lee, who bowed in apology with seven other senior Hong Kong officials.
Lee said Housing Secretary Winnie Ho had resigned on Wednesday, making her the first official to lose her job over the fire. Ho “should bear political responsibility” for the disaster, he said, despite no evidence of personal wrongdoing.
Lee also said the government would make changes to Hong Kong’s construction industry and regulatory system based on recommendations from a scathing report by a government-appointed independent committee that was also released Thursday.
The fire was the result of “decades of failure by the bodies in positions of responsibility in the construction, fire safety engineering and building management industries, and the Government,” according to the 1,154-page report , which was submitted to the government last week and was partially redacted upon its public release.
The long-awaited report found that the fire was most likely caused by a lit cigarette that ignited combustible materials nearby. During public hearings earlier this year, the committee heard testimony that construction workers had been smoking on site.
Renovation contractors also used non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets and flammable foam boards to cover windows, which put the “lives of all residents in WF Court at serious risk, apparently with a view to maximizing their financial gains,” the report said.
The report said that Prestige Construction & Engineering Co., the main contractor, and project consultant Will Power Architects Co. had “cut corners in numerous aspects.”
“There is no doubt that they are the main culprits responsible for the occurrence of the inferno and the high fatalities in the tragic incident,” it said.
Both companies, along with seven individuals, were criminally charged in June on 25 counts, including manslaughter, money laundering and tax evasion.
The report also took a broader view of Hong Kong’s building maintenance and renovation sector, citing a “corrupt eco-system” long characterized by practices such as bid-rigging, which it recommended be criminalized.
In addition, the report criticized the government over regulatory lapses and a “slack enforcement attitude” at the housing complex, where residents had repeatedly raised safety concerns.
“The Committee finds that no Government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues, and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum,” the report said.
Lee said Thursday that the Housing Bureau, Buildings Department, Fire Services Department and Labor Department all bore some responsibility for the blaze and that all four agencies would be the subject of a three-month investigation.
John Burns, a professor emeritus of politics and public administration at the University of Hong Kong, said it was “very significant” that Lee had apologized.
“We’ve gone for years with no chief executive talking about political accountability, as though it didn’t exist,” he told NBC News in an interview.
“Today, we have the chief executive talking about this directly and talking about a system of political accountability,” Burns said. “That’s a positive step.”
He added that it was “inevitable” that an official such as Ho would resign, “otherwise the credibility of the government itself would have been even more severely damaged.”
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.

The statement comes as Ukraine, Russia , and the U.S. prepare for another round of trilateral negotiations aimed at ending the war, with the sides yet to confirm a date for the meeting.
Hundreds of Ukrainian drones targeted Moscow overnight on Oct. 28-29, according to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, who said 613 drones had been launched toward the Russian capital.
"Our air defense systems are working effectively. But this shows once again that the situation continues, and the (war) must continue so that we are protected from threats," Peskov said.

The remarks come as diplomatic efforts to restart negotiations continue to face uncertainty.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Oct. 28 that the start of planned trilateral negotiations between Russia, the U.S., and Ukraine would depend on the situation on the battlefield.
The meeting was initially expected to take place in October, after U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukraine and Russia.
The visits yielded an agreement in principle to hold trilateral negotiations, but the Kremlin later declined to participate, accusing Kyiv of carrying out airstrikes on election day on Sept. 20.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 28 that he expects the planned negotiations to take place in mid-November, adding that Washington has yet to confirm a date.
The planned meeting follows a renewed U.S. effort to revive negotiations. Moscow has repeatedly rejected Western-backed proposals for a full and unconditional ceasefire, which Kyiv has supported, while continuing to demand that Ukraine cede Donbas .

articles.title_orig: Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
articles.title_zh: Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
articles.content_orig:
The chaos and horror of Spain's second rail tragedy this year has been conveyed vividly by survivors of Wednesday's high-speed crash that has left at least 69 people dead.
But as Spain holds three days of mourning, revelations from leaked audio recordings of the apparent human error in a control room in the minutes before this disaster happened have given way to public disbelief and outrage, in a highly politicised climate, exactly a month before Spaniards go to the polls.
"You don't know what's happening, you don't know what has happened, you just know that you're being thrown around in a matter of seconds," said Iñaki García, 60.
He was on the stationary Iryo train that was rammed from behind by a Renfe train on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140km (87 miles) south of the capital.
"There were people injured, walking around, there were dead people," he said. "In the next carriage along there were a lot of dead people."
Recalling the horrific scenes around him, one young man told the BBC in a quivering voice: "I don't know if that's something I'll ever recover from."
Stories of tragedy have continued to emerge. A pharmacist from Urda was one of the first to reach the scene, bringing with him first aid supplies and medicine.
"One of [the passengers] was saying goodbye to his wife and children. His last words were 'God is good'," Antonio García told Spanish radio.
Similar scenes of grief played out only nine months ago in the southern village of Adamuz, when a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people.
Now, in the town of Urda, just like Adamuz, awful stories are combined with acts of kindness and solidarity.
Locals turned out to help the injured, bringing blankets, food and water to a nearby sports hall that was converted into a makeshift hospital for much of the day.
"We all started to turn out to help and we organised ourselves as best we could," said Rosa María Domínguez, a local woman, who described the scene as "a horror film".
However, the overriding sentiment that these two tragedies have generated is one of confusion and a failure to comprehend how this could have happened.
Not long ago, the speed, efficiency and safety of Spain's high-speed rail system, the largest in Europe, was the envy of its neighbours.
The Adamuz crash triggered a nationwide debate about whether the network was fit for purpose.
This latest incident intensifies pressure on the left-wing government of Pedro Sánchez, in the middle of an election campaign where his Socialist PSOE is behind the conservatives in most opinion polls.
On Wednesday night a demonstration protesting at the government's handling of the rail network saw far-right groups turn out and clash with police.
Although the main parties, other than the far-right Vox, have suspended campaigning, Sánchez has twice visited the scene of the crash and his People's Party rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo came to Urda on Thursday.
Sánchez's transport minister, Óscar Puente, made clear from the start that a computer failure followed by human error was the likely cause of the crash. By late evening, leaked audio recordings of a control-room operator talking to train drivers appeared to back that up.
Puente has long been a hate figure for the right, and with two of the worst rail tragedies in Spanish history taking place on his watch, the criticism is only going to increase.
Spain's biggest train drivers' union Semaf condemned the leak of audio recordings as irresponsible and slanted. The union had already called a strike for Thursday in a bid to ensure that "urgency to travel is never prioritised over safety".
One train driver, Vicente Almenar, told Spanish media: "They always look for the last link in the chain, where it's weakest, but here the entire procedure failed because we don't even know what our colleague was seeing on the screen," he told Spanish media.
Sánchez had not been expecting rail safety to dominate his campaign, but that now looks increasingly likely.
After two accidents and more than 100 deaths on the same high-speed line, Feijóo told reporters in Urda on Thursday: "The Spanish people need answers. They are wondering what is happening to high-speed rail in their country."
And he emphasised that politics was not about talking - it was about acting.

eaked PlayStation Store backend data indicates that Grand Theft Auto VI will reportedly require a massive 210 GB install size
Physical editions of the game are expected to package digital download codes rather than optical discs
Pre-loading is rumored to open on November 12 ahead of a November 19 console launch priced at $79.99 USD
PlayStation and Xbox listings have reportedly revealed that Grand Theft Auto VI will require an immense 210 GB file size upon release. According to database scraper PlayStation Game Size , the leak outlines substantial storage demands ahead of launch.
Reports from the scraped database backend reveal that the standard edition of the highly anticipated title is rumored to take up 210 GB of internal storage across both PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles. Physical copies are also reported to ship with digital download codes rather than optical discs. While console editions are lined up for the initial launch, reports suggest a PC edition is slated to follow in early 2027.
The standard edition of Grand Theft Auto VI is rumored to release on November 19 at midnight local time for $79.99 USD, with pre-loading reportedly opening on November 12 via the PlayStation Store.

articles.title_zh: Airbnb pledges $500M to nonprofit, scaling emergency stays and raising questions over housing relief
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Airbnb is committing $500 million to its philanthropic arm over the next five years to expand temporary housing assistance for medical travelers and disaster survivors.
The short-term rental platform will fund this initiative by contributing 10 cents from every booking and covering any remaining gap, according to Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky.
Airbnb.org, an independent nonprofit whose operational costs the company already covers, aims to scale up to provide 1 million nights of free lodging annually.
The pledge, announced Wednesday, comes amid an uncertain climate for corporate philanthropy.
A recent survey by Chief Executives for Corporate Purpose showed most companies reduced charitable contributions over the past five years, driven by changes in tax law.
Airbnb.org's updated funding framework has renewed questions about the charitable efforts of a business criticized by affordable housing advocates for reducing the availability of lower-cost residential homes.
Critics argue the broader housing crisis, exacerbated by short-term rentals, leaves fewer options for people displaced by disasters.
The dynamic highlights a debate over whether for-profit companies should use philanthropy to offset negative business impacts. Major artificial intelligence firms, currently drafting plans to distribute a portion of their wealth, maintain that they should.
For Chesky, the answer is an emphatic "no." He rejected claims that Airbnb drives up city housing costs, though he admitted some hosts take a small fraction of local housing off the market.
He described the commitment as doing the "right thing" with the platform's "natural superpower."
"I don’t like this idea that somehow you create a nonprofit to make up for or apologize for your core business," Chesky told The Associated Press. "Our core business, independently, is gonna affect a lot more lives than this organization. And our core business needs to be responsible. And if we’re doing something that’s not responsible, we need to correct it."
Governments including Spain and New York City have recently introduced measures to limit short-term rentals. Karolina Mikołajewska-Zając, a postdoctoral fellow at Copenhagen Business School who studies digital platforms, suggested the company could use its expanding philanthropic footprint to further integrate into communities and legitimize short-term rentals as its model faces challenges.
She warned the humanitarian sector against becoming overly dependent on commercial platforms.
Murray Cox, founder of the data activist project Inside Airbnb, noted one key crisis omitted from the nonprofit's list of emergency relief efforts.
"There’s also the housing crisis that’s occurring around the world," Cox said. "And, although they’re not causing the housing crisis, they’re contributing to it by taking millions of housing units — residential houses — off the housing market."

articles.title_orig: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.title_zh: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
While Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) stock is getting crushed on Thursday after earnings, Microsoft ( MSFT ) is getting a pass. Another way of saying it: Microsoft shares aren't trading down in sympathy. And there is one simple reason why this is the case.
Microsoft's quarter is being seen as one of higher-than-expected growth that is sustainable, while Alphabet's quarter was sluggish and hinted at slowing growth rates in coming quarters.
Microsoft's Azure sales growth came in about 300 basis points above analyst estimates. Overall sales for the important cloud business grew 48%, excluding currency fluctuations. Execs guided to 49% to 50% Azure sales growth in the current quarter, ahead of consensus estimates by four percentage points.
The company's capex came in about $5 billion below estimates, and other parts of the business showed sales upside. Sales and earnings for the quarter came in ahead of analyst forecasts.
"Net/net, these results increase our confidence in the company's ability to sustain mid/upper-teens revenue growth and that strong cost of goods sold/expense operational efficiencies should be supportive of expanding operating margins," said stifel analyst Brad Reback.
Alphabet shares tanked 11% after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown, both on its own and versus Microsoft.
First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.
Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate of negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's ( META ) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), Google's print stunk up the joint.
"Alphabet's 3Q results reinforced concerns we had heading into the print, re: Search is decelerating and margins have peaked near-term. This could create an air pocket over the next 1-2 quarters as investors await signs for whether this is transitory or structural," KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson said.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu falls short of majority as Israel faces three possible paths to a new government
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu falls short of majority as Israel faces three possible paths to a new government
articles.content_orig:
As coalition negotiations loom and allegations of foreign election interference emerge, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Tel Aviv, Israel.
TEL AVIV, Israel - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition remained well short of a parliamentary majority Thursday as newly counted ballots showed a dramatic surge in support for Arab parties, potentially giving the opposition enough votes to challenge his control of parliament.
With 93.8% of ballots counted as of 4 a.m. ET Thursday (10 a.m. local time in Israel), including votes from the double-envelope count, Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc was projected to win 53 seats in Israel's 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. The two predominantly Arab parties were projected to secure a combined 19 seats, bringing the potential anti-Netanyahu parliamentary majority to 67.
The updated figures showed Netanyahu's Likud remaining the largest individual party with 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar party with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad party with 12. The figures remain preliminary.
NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on Oct. 20, 2026. (Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images)
The results leave neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with the 61 seats required to form a government independently, raising the prospect of difficult coalition negotiations or another election.
The biggest shift came from Israel's Arab voters, whose turnout surged compared with previous elections, potentially reshaping the country's political balance.
Arab voter participation reached approximately 80%, compared with 53.2% in the 2022 election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute . The 2026 figure remains preliminary.
The Joint List was projected to win 11 seats, while Ra'am was projected to secure eight. Together, their 19 seats would nearly double the Arab parties' representation from the 10 seats they won in 2022.
Overall voter turnout reached 77.7% by the official 10 p.m. closing time on election night, the highest level at that hour since 1999, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee.
The increased Arab participation could prove decisive in determining the next government's composition. Although Eisenkot and several other opposition leaders ruled out including Arab parties in their governing coalition during the campaign, their parliamentary support could allow the opposition to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, and gain greater control over the legislative agenda even before a new government is formed.
IRAN IS TRYING TO ‘CREATE A ROT FROM WITHIN’ THROUGH ‘INFORMATION WARFARE,’ ANALYST WARNS
Posters of Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu are displayed on billboards ahead of the Knesset elections, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 25, 2026. (Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
The political stakes intensified Thursday following a Channel 12 report alleging that substantial sums originating in Qatar may have been transferred to influence voter participation in Arab communities.
According to N12, some of the funds allegedly traveled through financial channels previously used to transfer money to terrorist organizations , including currency exchanges.
The allegations have not been independently substantiated, and investigators have yet to establish whether foreign financing occurred or whether election-related crimes were committed.
Channel 12 reported that Shin Bet Director David Zini presented intelligence concerning suspected foreign interference to Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, prompting the judge to order an investigation.
In a letter published by N12 , Sohlberg instructed the domestic security agency to investigate the allegations and identify evidence that could either substantiate or disprove them. He requested findings within one week, citing the limited time available during the election count.
The judge's letter did not publicly identify Qatar as the suspected foreign actor. That identification came from N12's reporting.
Qatar strongly denied the allegations Thursday, accusing Israeli politicians of attempting to drag the Gulf nation into Israel's domestic political disputes following the election.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr. Majed Al-Ansari wrote on X.
Al-Ansari accused Israeli politicians and their allies in the media of launching a "disinformation campaign," saying Qatar had been accused of financing Netanyahu, the Israeli left and now Arab voters.
"If these claims were to be believed, Qatar would apparently own all of Israel," he wrote. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians," Al-Ansari added, insisting that Qatar had no involvement in Israel's electoral process and would continue its diplomatic and humanitarian efforts in the region.
Acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne also rejected the allegations in a letter to Yesh Atid MK Vladimir Beliak, who sits on the committee. "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
But the allegations quickly became part of the political confrontation over whether opposition parties should cooperate with Arab lawmakers.
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW
An Arab-Israeli woman casts her ballot during Israel's general elections on Oct. 27, 2026, in Umm El Fahem, Israel. (Amir Levy/Getty Images)
Netanyahu and Likud had already challenged the legitimacy of the Arab parties' electoral gains. On Wednesday, before the latest Qatari allegations emerged, Likud accused Arab parties of stealing the election through alleged voter fraud, accusations that had not been substantiated.
In a statement Thursday, Likud argued that the suspected foreign interference made cooperation with the Arab parties unacceptable.
"After it became clear that foreign actors attempted to take control of the Knesset, it is obvious that no Zionist party must cooperate with Ra'am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker using votes bought with cash, or establish a government dangerous to Israel," the party said.
The assertion that parliamentary seats were obtained through purchased votes has not been established by the investigation.
Hauser Tov, a political reporter for Israel's Haaretz newspaper, argued on X that the statement revealed Likud's immediate political objective: preventing the opposition from using its potential parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker.
Israeli journalist Amir Tibon wrote on X, "The main reason they want to prevent this is so that the Knesset won't vote to establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7." He argued that such an investigation could examine Qatari involvement in Gaza and Israel.
Eisenkot responded to the allegations Thursday, after meeting with Israel Security Agency (Shin Bet) Director David Zini. "Foreign involvement in Israel is unacceptable and profoundly serious, particularly when it involves a country that funds and supports Hamas," Eisenkot said. "It is serious when it occurs in the Prime Minister’s Office, and it is serious if it occurs in the electoral process."
He called on the Shin Bet to investigate the allegations thoroughly and take the strongest possible action against anyone found to have attempted to compromise the election's integrity.

articles.title_orig: RFK Jr. to Allow Broad Use of Unapproved Peptide Injections
articles.title_zh: RFK Jr. to Allow Broad Use of Unapproved Peptide Injections
articles.content_orig:
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. has released plans to loosen restrictions on controversial peptides.
The plans, which were announced in the US Federal Register on Wednesday, say Kennedy would allow compounding pharmacies to prepare six popular peptides, which have not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
In an unusual move, the draft came from the office of the health secretary rather than the FDA. After the plan has been officially published later this week, there will be a two-week public comment period.
Unregulated injectable peptides have become popular online. Experts have warned of their lack of clinical trials for humans and unknown long-term effects.
The peptides mentioned in the plan include BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c and Semax. Compounding pharmacies will be able to mix them to create medications.
The BBC has contacted the FDA for comment.
An FDA advisory panel voted in July to loosen restrictions on the six peptides. But FDA staff members recommended against it.
Kennedy has described himself as a "big fan" of the drugs and has previously vowed to ease restrictions on them after the Biden administration clamped down on the growing industry.
Peptides are short chains of amino acids, or small proteins, which our bodies naturally produce. They act as messengers, telling cells what to do, and play vital roles in skin health, immune system and hormone regulation.
Peptides have been used to treat medical conditions for more than a century. Insulin, one of the first peptide hormones to be discovered, helps people with Type 1 diabetes and some with Type 2 manage their blood sugar levels.
But now unregulated peptides have exploded onto the wellness market since GLP-1s, weight loss drugs, became mainstream.
Online influencers have been marketing peptides in what they have called "stacks" for unproven uses, claiming they can be used as a quick way to help people look younger, heal or improve their skin.
They have become popular among teens on TikTok, especially boys, over unproven claims they help to build muscle, part of online trends known as "biohacking" and "looksmaxxing".
Health experts have cautioned against use of the drugs, citing a lack of clinical trials for humans and the unknown long-term effects of the substances.

articles.title_orig: ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Destroys A Playercount Record On Steam
articles.title_zh: ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Destroys A Playercount Record On Steam
articles.content_orig:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Travis Northup. He loves action RPGs, including Phantom Blade Zero. Read his review here .
I play an obscene amount of soulslikes and sweaty action games, and although I largely enjoy my time facing off against these intentionally challenging gauntlets, one thing I’ve grown increasingly irritated by in recent years is something I’ve taken to calling the Scrub Tax .
But what is the Scrub Tax exactly? Well, it can take many forms. Sometimes it’s a nearly minute-long walk back to the lair of the boss I’m trying to beat. Or maybe it’s a super obnoxious unskippable cutscene I’m forced to watch every time you beat the boss’ first phase as they transform into an even more gruesome monster. Other times, it’s just a good ol’-fashioned 30-second loading screen that has me rubbing my temples in annoyance between failed runs. In other words, the Scrub Tax is an irritating procedure (intentional or otherwise) that games make you go through after getting yourself killed like the low-skill scrub that you are – things that waste your time unnecessarily beyond the hours you’re already investing in learning the encounter and “gitting gud.”
Phantom Blade Zero, though, shows us it doesn’t need to be this way, just by sprinkling a little sugar over the medicine that so many modern boss battles force you to swallow — Mary Poppins would be so proud.
Don’t get me wrong: I love getting my butt kicked in every single FromSoftware game – learning the attacks of some horrifying new foe and slowly building confidence after multiple deaths before utterly dominating the enemy is an impressively compelling loop. But I’m much less enthusiastic about the tiresome ways in which my time is wasted while I’m working to hone my skills. It’s already an odd choice to make players go through this kind of stuff in an era when more things are competing for our attention than ever before, but it’s an especially bizarre thing to include when you’ve specifically designed a game with repeated failure in mind .
This brings me to one of the most infuriating forms the Scrub Tax takes: a complete lack of checkpoints during boss fights. Nowadays it’s not just common, but almost universally accepted that if I die at any point in any phase of a boss fight, I should have to start over again from the very beginning. This means that every player is destined to spend significantly more time replaying through less exciting phases of these encounters than the later phases that are actually still challenging them. I can’t even count the number of times I’ve been excited for a final confrontation with a boss I’ve crawled over hot coals to face, only to find myself irritated 20 minutes later when I’m grinding through the first phase of the encounter for the 10th time, just so I can enjoy about 30 seconds of the second phase I keep dying on.
For example, I have a vivid memory of playing Lies of P for the first time and facing off against an extremely cool and challenging boss that had a very slow first phase. What should have been a highlight instead became incredibly frustrating. I’d fought my way through that first phase dozens of times, to the point where I’d done several completions of it in a row where I didn’t even take damage, effectively shifting gear into autopilot for the three minutes it took to get through it. By the time I finally did beat the final phase of this boss, I was so vexed at having over half of my time wasted repeating the first one that I couldn’t even enjoy my hard-fought victory.
This practice has become so shockingly common that I don’t even think most people understand just how much of their time is being wasted by these tedious roadblocks. In fact, this philosophy of game design has been so ingrained into my expectations that until I recently played through Phantom Blade Zero, it didn’t even occur to me just how much of a thorn in my side this has become. I can count on one hand the number of games that haven’t followed this format over the past decade, the most notable being Final Fantasy XVI, which isn’t really all that concerned with providing the player a challenge. God of War Ragnarok included the choice to turn on checkpoints for certain boss fights as an accessibility setting, which is an interesting option for those not wishing to bang their head up against a wall repeatedly, but I’m referring to a more specific niche of players who crave a tough fight and simply don’t want their time wasted. For people like me, having precious hours eaten up by tedious boss checkpoint design has simply become an accepted cost of doing business for a long time now.
Phantom Blade Zero has shattered the idea that this is just the way it has to be. Developer S-Game’s stellar action RPG succeeds not just because it’s full of badass, challenging boss fights that show off its grade-A combat, but because failure doesn’t cost you momentum. It trims a ton of fat and empty calories by making it easy to get right back into its showpiece showdowns. This improves its overall pacing massively. Instead of spending twice as long as you should on each boss fight, you work through each one at an incredibly steady clip, move on to the next obstacle faster, and, frankly, have more fun in the process. The 50 hours it took me to get through my first playthrough was such a refreshing experience; it made me increasingly irate that more games don’t choose to handle boss encounters this way.
“But Travis, adding checkpoints to boss fights trivializes difficulty, and we like difficulty.”
I agree that difficulty is a good thing! But if the only way you’re able to make your encounter difficult is by bloating its duration with multiple phases, effectively turning it into a test of patience as much as skill, then you have not created a very engaging boss battle. This kind of difficulty is aggravating because it’s so patently artificial . Most of the time I’m not being challenged at all by an opening phase that I’ve more or less committed to memory after a few runs – the challenge is in having the stamina to engage in the Sisyphean task of replaying the same series of blocks, parries, and dodges ad nauseam.
Wouldn’t it be nice if, by removing the need to replay prior phases, developers really took the gloves off and made those later rounds as brutal as their wicked hearts desired? Imagine a boss fight where half the attacks kill you instantly, and you don’t even mind because you’re only losing a handful of seconds with every failed run. I want to live in a world where instead of being punished as I go through the completely normal process of learning an encounter, every failure has almost zero friction to it.
Phantom Blade Zero is a fantastic reference point for this, because even when some of my deaths felt cheap (like attacks that killed me in one hit), it was incredibly easy to shrug off since I was instantly thrown right back into the action. PBZ’s philosophy of checkpointing bosses meant that I was less irritated by enemies who had ludicrously powerful attacks. That allows S-Game to experiment more with boss scenarios that simply would not fly in a game without checkpoints where the developers know each death is going to cost upwards of five minutes of your time. A death in Phantom Blade Zero is likely to cost you less than 30 seconds, so when the crazy badass warrior with a lightning spear impaled me on his weapon and launched me into space, I relished the loss and jumped right back into the fight. I want developers to be able to take more chances with boss encounters, and checkpointing is a truly powerful tool that allows them to do just that. By freeing us from repetition, it also unshackles the developer’s creativity.
Even if you think restarting from the beginning is something devs should keep around, surely there are better ways to handle this unnecessary Scrub Tax, right? For example, shouldn’t I be able to skip the first phase of a boss fight after I’ve managed to clear it wit

articles.title_orig: Rare love letters to French aristocrat shed light on Louis XVI maritime mystery
articles.title_zh: Rare love letters to French aristocrat shed light on Louis XVI maritime mystery
articles.content_orig:
‘Miracle’ cache of letters written by French scientist who died in ill-fated La Pérouse mission give personal account of 1785 voyage
As he prepared to climb the scaffolding to be publicly executed by guillotine on 21 January 1793, Louis XVI is reported to have asked: “Is there news of Monsieur de la Pérouse?”
He was referring to Jean-François de Galaup, the count of Pérouse , a naval officer and navigator whom the French king had dispatched in 1785 on a round-the-world scientific mission to rival discoveries made by the English explorer Captain James Cook.
The two ships under La Pérouse’s command, La Boussole and L’Astrolabe, disappeared three years later after leaving Botany Bay in Australia. The wrecks were only formally identified in 2005 and exactly what happened to them remains a mystery to this day.
Now rare letters written by an illustrious scientist who perished in 1788 have resurfaced, giving a new and personal account of the voyage. They are described as veiled love letters addressed to the married daughter of an aristocratic family, and were discovered hidden in a book of engravings being examined in preparation for auction.
Ludovic Miran, a book and manuscript expert for the auctioneers selling the letters next month, described the find as “a miracle”.
“We have a certain number of documents from the expedition but they are almost all scientific, so these personal letters are extremely rare,” Miran told the Guardian. “They throw a completely new light on what is in France an extraordinary scientific and historical event.”
The La Pérouse expedition was launched at a time when Britain and France were in a period of intense rivalry over colonial expansion. La Pérouse was a great admirer of Cook and his maritime mapping and scientific discoveries, but Louis XVI had more political and trade ambitions. The French wanted to create trade routes and discover whether the secret information they had that Britain was planning to establish a permanent base at Botany Bay, giving it access to unexplored areas of the Pacific region, was correct.
La Pérouse’s ships, carrying 225 crew, officers and scientists, sailed from Brest on France’s Atlantic coast on 1 August 1785 and for almost three years sent reports during stopovers including from Alaska, California, Asia, Russia and Samoa, where the captain of the Astrolabe and 11 men were killed.
At the time of Louis XVI’s execution, there had been no news of the frigates since their departure from Botany Bay in March 1788. To La Pérouse’s dismay, Captain Arthur Phillip and Britain’s First Fleet had beaten him to the Australian coast – inhabited by an Indigenous population for tens of thousands of years – by just six days.
La Boussole and L’Astrolabe are believed to have foundered on coral reefs at Vanikoro east of the Solomon Islands during a tornado a few months later. Wreckage was discovered in 1826 and 1964 but only formally identified in 2005.
The letters were written by Jean-André Mongez, a brilliant scientist, director of an illustrious science revue and church canon who was with the expedition, to Louise Victoire Le Cloustier, the daughter of a minor noble family from Rouen, Normandy.
Miran said Mongez used the letters to express his unhappiness at her marriage and appears to repent for previous bad behaviour. “He writes several times: ‘I will be back, I will be another man, a better man’,” Miran said. “One has the impression he has not behaved well towards her and she has put him in his place.”
This may, he added, have been behind Mongez’s decision to undertake such a long and perilous journey. “The references are often veiled, but they seem to have had a very close relationship but he seems to have caused some offence at some point. They are intimate, very personal letters,” he said.
“He tells her he is leaving ‘a bit for the love of fame and the desire to acquire new knowledge’, but he already had scientific glory and a good career and they would have all read James Cook’s works before leaving so they knew about the dangers.
after newsletter promotion
“We will never know why he decided to join this perilous journey, but it is clear he was leaving in part because of this emotional relationship.”
Miran added: “The correspondence also provides answers as to how these young men endured three years of navigation around the world, a completely new and unimaginable experience. We learn how they withstood the shock of such a crazy journey and horrible conditions.
“He recounts how his friend and others were massacred on one stop. In his last letter he tells her the expedition has taken a sad turn and he now only wants to come home because such unhappiness is not compensated for by the meagre scientific results they have.
“Perhaps it is a journey of redemption.”
Le Cloustier died in 1821, like the rest of the world unaware of the fate of Mongez or the expedition. “But she kept the letters and we can tell they have been read, and reread. I would imagine she had to hide them from her husband,” Miran said.
The auctioneer Benoît Derouineau said he had discovered the letters in an “unremarkable” 19th-century book of engravings being prepared for sale.
“I didn’t realise what they were at first. They had clearly been carefully saved and hidden. Perhaps because they were a kind of love letter and the recipient didn’t want them seen. But she hadn’t thrown them away or burned them,” he said.
“That Louis XVI is said to have asked about La Pérouse shows how much was invested in this expedition. It was a very important event in France.”
The letters, valued at €30,000-€50,000, are being sold as one lot by Daguerre at the Hôtel Drouot, Paris, on 17 November.

articles.title_orig: Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices
articles.title_zh: Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices
articles.content_orig:
Footage shows Thomas Markle's son handing over VHS tapes and dismantled computers to police
Philippine police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from the former home of Thomas Markle, father of the Duchess of Sussex.
Earlier this month, it was reported that hundreds of images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle Sr, 82, had been found at the property in the Philippines.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr, who is now in the US, has strongly denied the allegations made by his son, describing them as "sick lies".
Cebu Regional Prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that Thomas Markle Jr was "adamant" that the case should be investigated, and that he felt his father "has to answer for it".
Last week, the Sun on Sunday reported that Thomas Markle Sr's ex-wife, Roslyn Loveless, had sent a letter to the Metropolitan Police about the 2019 allegations, which was shared with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time.
Loveless, who has since died, is the mother of Meghan's two half-siblings. She divorced Thomas Markle Sr. in 1975, before he married the duchess's mother.
Thomas Markle Sr strongly denies the allegations of possessing images of child sexual abuse
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a statement shared on Friday, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".
Speaking to the Sun, Thomas Markle Jr also apologised to Meghan for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement, and said he had "been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years".
Thomas Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May.
He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
The police say they must identify how the material was obtained before they can consider any criminal charges.
Campaigners describe Cebu as a known hotspot for the sexual exploitation of children, and authorities say they take any such allegations very seriously.

articles.title_orig: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 passengers, mostly Americans, are stranded in Cambodia after the operator of a luxury U.S. cruise ship that was on a continuous around-the-world voyage ran out of money due to skyrocketing fuel costs .
Villa Vie Residences, the Florida-based operator of the MV Odyssey, said the war with Iran quadrupled fuel costs and forced it to suspend operations on Tuesday.
CEO Mikael Petterson told CBS News in a phone interview Wednesday that Villa Vie Residences was paying an average of $700 a ton for fuel before the war broke out in late February. Since then, it has been paying anywhere from $2,000 to $3,000 per ton.
The Odyssey uses between 700 and 800 tons per month in fuel, Petterson disclosed.
"When you divide it over 300 people on board, it's just backbreaking," Petterson told CBS News. "And this has been going on for nine months. We've tried to do everything we can do."
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences said the per cabin fuel costs rose from an average of $1,800 per month before the war to between $6,000 and $8,000.
The company was unwilling to pass those rising costs on to its passengers, Petterson said.
The Odyssey launched in October 2024 for a continuous around-the-world journey. At the time, passengers could become residents of the ship by purchasing a permanent cabin for several hundred thousand dollars. Some sold their homes to do so. At the time, they were given a 15-year minimum guarantee of residency aboard the Odyssey.
The Odyssey attempted to counter the spiking fuel prices by slowing down its itinerary and spending five or six days in each port "hoping that things would come to a close in the Middle East," Petterson said, but it wasn't enough.
"For us, when our monthly expenses go up from $400,000 to $2 million, where are we going to get the $1.6 million?" Petterson asked.
The Villa Vie Residences CEO said that the ship ran out of money as it searched for a financial partner, and the plan is now to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
"We've borrowed money, we've stretched our payrolls as far as we can, and we're at a point where it's just at a breaking point where we need capitalization," Petterson said.
Passenger Benjamin Schatz thought the MV Odyssey would be his forever home.
"Honestly, right now, I'm in denial and in shock, and I'm heartbroken," Schatz, a retiree, told CBS News.
CBS News met Schatz in April 2025 for a story featuring Villa Vie Residences. At that point, he had been living on the ship for about one year. On Wednesday, he was given just hours to pack up his life and leave.
Said Schatz: "There are people now who are homeless and who have very little money and don't know what they're going to do."

articles.title_orig: After Reinventing Mathematics, Can A.I. Eradicate Computer Bugs?
articles.title_zh: After Reinventing Mathematics, Can A.I. Eradicate Computer Bugs?
articles.content_orig:
Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper , is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.
For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior .
Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.
“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”
&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.
And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.
The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.
The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.
Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.
Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc .
Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.
Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.
But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.
Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.
Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.
Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.
Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.
Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face , he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”
Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.
But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means
articles.title_zh: Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Iran war continues to weigh on Americans' wallets, and it's costing them more in increased fuel costs than consumers in any other country in the world, new data finds. As President Donald Trump argues the cost of the war will be justified with economic prosperity, his administration may be pushing policies making the problem worse.
U.S. consumers have paid an average of $471 more in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran war in February, according to a report published on Monday by Finland-based nonprofit research institute Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). That's nearly eight times greater than the average of about $60 in increased energy costs per person globally. As a country, the U.S. has spent $160 billion total on increased fuel costs since the beginning of the war, with China following at $54 billion, and Canada coming in third at $17 billion.
The Iran war has cost U.S. households about $2,000 , according to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, a sum that includes both soaring prices at the gas pump as well as increased airfares and inflation as a result of increased transportation expenses and supply-chain shuffles over the last seven months of Middle East turmoil.
Trump has repeatedly tried to assuage Americans' anxieties about increased costs associated with the war. At a rally in North Carolina in September, the president downplayed affordability concerns . He has argued the war is necessary to prevent Iran from attaining nuclear weapons, and that the U.S. is making a " freaking fortune " as a result of increased energy production.
"It's a very inexpensive price to pay for what we've done," Trump said last month of fuel costs, which have now topped $4.26 per gallon, up from $2.98 before the war. "Remember that."
The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune 's request for comment.
To be sure, the Iran war did not create the conditions under which American consumers in particular are paying higher energy costs. While global supply strains have increased fuel prices globally, the outsize impact on U.S. consumers is a result of an American economy and culture structured around oil.
"If you compare the U.S. with countries in Europe with similar levels of income, you can really see the effect of decades of lower prices for fuel and less emphasis on sustainable transportation," CREA cofounder and report author Lauri Myllyvirta told Fortune . "Undoing that, of course, takes quite a bit of time and effort."
The U.S. is heavily exposed to higher fuel costs in part because it is beholden to global market rates, a result of it still having to trade for heavy oil despite being a major diesel producer. But the heavier energy burden on American consumers is mostly because of the country's reliance on oil over other sustainable means of energy, CREA argued.
The U.S. has less electric-vehicle adoption than other countries. And less efficient gas-powered cars travel farther on American roads compared to other countries, meaning American consumers simply burn more fuel than consumers in other countries, the report said. CREA found a positive correlation between countries with the greatest EV market share—Norway, Sweden, Finland, the Netherlands, and Belgium—and fuel cost savings per person.
Across the world, EV sales have surged as fuel costs have increased. In Denmark, for example, EVs made up 81% of new-vehicle sales in the first eight months of 2026. Nearly all new-vehicle sales in Norway over the same period were EVs, and 57% of new-vehicle sales in China were all-electric. Some European countries such as Germany saw a decrease in gas and diesel demand in 2026.
By comparison, only 7.3% of new-vehicle sales in the U.S. over that span were plug-in EVs, and the report found that American drivers who made the switch to eclectic cars saw only a $17 increase in charging costs since early March as a result of electricity price increases.
Myllyvirta suggested this pattern is primed to continue. A series of U.S. policy changes has disincentivized Americans from purchasing EVs and automakers from building fuel efficient vehicles.
The Trump administration ended a $7,500 tax credit on new EVs in September 2025 it claimed would devastate the auto industry. Analysts have cited the end of the incentive as the reason EV demand flattened in the U.S., and the reason why companies like Ford rolled back production on all-electric cars in favor of hybrid vehicles.
Last month, Trump released new fuel economy standards , loosening Biden-era regulatory requirements for fuel efficiency to mitigate pollution—a move the president said would make cars more affordable, but that environmentalists argued would drive up fuel costs and cancel out any vehicle savings.
According to Myllyvirta, increased fuel costs for Americans are poised to continue, even if the war ends. While energy prices will level out once this conflict is over, the reliance on gas-powered cars will mean a repetition of this cycle during the next energy shock.
"The only certainty is volatility," he said. "Prices are going to come down, and then there are going to be new shocks. And as long as the reliance on oil continues, that cycle is going to play out with effects on consumers, with effects on inflation and economic policy."
This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles.title_orig: Why is Russia sending fighter jets and air defences to Ethiopia?
articles.title_zh: Why is Russia sending fighter jets and air defences to Ethiopia?
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will acquire four S-400 air defence batteries, in a deal experts say strengthens Moscow’s foothold in the Horn of Africa while bolstering Addis Ababa’s military amid conflict at home and tensions with neighbouring Eritrea.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the deal in Moscow during the two-day Russia-Africa Summit .
“I value the friendly relations between Russia and Ethiopia,” Russian President Vladimir Putin said in a statement. “Russia and Ethiopia stand together in international affairs.”
Experts say the agreement builds on decades of military cooperation, offering Moscow arms revenue and diplomatic influence while allowing Ethiopia to strengthen its armed forces amid its ongoing conflict in Tigray.
Abiy said Ethiopia had taken delivery of its first 12 Su-35s under an earlier agreement with Russia, with four S-400 batteries to follow, but did not say when the air defence systems would arrive.
The aircraft would expand an air force already equipped with Russian fighter jets. The S-400 systems would complement this existing fleet by helping the military defend itself against aerial threats, experts say.
“They would be best used against conventional air threats,” Benedict Manzin, a lead analyst on the Middle East and Africa at risk consultancy Sibylline, told Al Jazeera. “In a war with Eritrea, they could be used against Eritrea’s limited air force and drones.”
However, air defences do not provide protection against every kind of attack.
“As we have seen in Ukraine, conventional air defence systems can be overwhelmed by small, cheap drones,” he said.
The relationship predates the current competition for influence in Africa.
“Russia has been engaged in Ethiopia for decades, part of the legacy of the Cold War,” Manzin said.
The Soviet Union backed Ethiopia’s former communist government. Today’s cooperation builds on those foundations, with the two countries having signed military agreements intended to improve the Ethiopian armed forces’ capabilities through technology, knowledge and training, according to the Ethiopian News Agency.
Commercial interests also matter.
“Russia is also in the business of making money through arms sales,” Manzin said. “This is one of Russia’s primary exports to Africa.”
Weapons sales provide revenue while sustaining relationships with governments that require training, maintenance and replacement equipment. But the partnership extends beyond defence.
Abiy said his talks with Putin covered nuclear energy, health and trade, alongside bilateral and multilateral cooperation, while in a statement, Putin said bilateral trade exceeded $1.3bn in January-September, more than twice the figure for all of 2025.
He identified energy, agriculture, industry and education among potential areas for further cooperation.
Ethiopia’s size also makes it attractive to competing powers, with experts saying that because it is Africa’s second-most populous country, it offers a substantial market.
“Everyone engages a bit, and Ethiopia tries to maximise its gains,” Manzin said.
Manzin suggested Ethiopia is widening its options rather than committing exclusively to Moscow.
“African states are aware that they are a focus of geopolitical competition,” he said.
That competition gives governments room to seek weapons, investment and diplomatic backing from different partners. Ethiopia’s relationship with Russia coexists with a significant Chinese presence and continuing Western investment in the country.
“China has a huge presence in Ethiopia, and Russian arms have always been a huge factor,” Manzin said. Moscow is seeking to turn those established connections into broader influence as Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine constrain its international relationships.
Russia supplied 15 percent of African imports of major weapons in 2021–2025, behind the United States at 19 percent and China at 17 percent, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
In his statement, Abiy thanked Putin for ensuring the aircraft were delivered a year ahead of schedule and said the equipment would strengthen Ethiopia’s ability to “preemptively deter aggression”.
The delivery comes amid renewed fighting in Tigray, a separate rebellion in Amhara and concerns about a possible conflict with Eritrea.
“Ethiopia is buying a lot of aircraft,” Manzin said. “The timing comes as Ethiopia is going through conflict in Tigray, with speculation about war with Eritrea.”
He cautioned against assuming the latest battlefield developments directly prompted purchases negotiated earlier.
“Aircraft are helpful regardless, as they are using aircraft and the air force heavily during any suppression,” he said.
Fighting between Ethiopia’s federal army and Tigrayan forces intensified in late September, in effect unravelling the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war.
Each side has blamed the other for renewed violence. Tensions grew following the formation of a seven-group alliance seeking to overthrow Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration.
Government troops and allied forces entered Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, earlier in October after Tigray People’s Liberation Front ( TPLF ) fighters withdrew.
Addis Ababa subsequently installed a six-month caretaker administration, but rebel commanders have promised to continue fighting.

articles.title_orig: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment, say regulators
articles.title_zh: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment, say regulators
articles.content_orig:
South West Water has been given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency over high levels of pollution.
The regulator downgraded the firm from two stars out of a possible four to one, meaning it is now considered a "poor performing company" for its environmental impact.
It said it had performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents for the 15th year in a row.
South West Water, which has 1.8 million customers across Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of Dorset and Somerset, said it knew there was "much more to do" and was taking action to improve areas that "matter most" to customers and the environment.
The annual Environmental Performance Assessment grades England's nine water and sewerage companies largely on how often they pollute rivers, streams and the sea.
For 2025, South West Water was among four companies rated as poor performing, or one star, while four others were rated as requiring improvement, two stars.
South West Water performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents [BBC]
Severn Trent Water was the only company to achieve the highest rating of four stars.
The Environment Agency's report card comes a month after South West Water was fined almost £8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years.
In the last year it also recorded the sharpest rise in customer complaints of any water company .
Serious incidents in the past year include pollution in St Austell River , killing thousands of fish, while pollution at Exmouth meant beachgoers had to leave the water .
Industry regulator Ofwat said the company met seven of its 23 targets in 2025-26, with below target performance for "most areas".
It noted its performance in relation to water supply interruptions "deteriorated substantially" and, despite improving annual performance by 38%, said the company's total pollution incidents performance remained more than double its target.
Customer satisfaction also remained challenging, ranking 15 out of 17 in the sector.
While storm overflows performance improved by 19%, it still fell short of its target, the Environment Agency said.
It was, however, the only company to have met its target for internal sewer flooding, or how often wastewater enters a property, every year since 2020-21.
A spokesperson for South West Water said: "We are under new management with a renewed focus on improving our performance.
"We know there's much more to do and although it will take time, we are taking action and making progress in the areas that matter most to our customers and the environment."
They said the firm had "reduced spills from storm overflows by 17% last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%, and we have insourced over 40 new leakage specialists".
"We are working hard to build on the progress we're making, backed by record levels of investment across the region," the spokesperson said.
"We are transforming our network to improve long-term resilience of our water supply; protecting the environment and tackling leaks as part of our multibillion-pound plan to deliver the long-term improvements our customers and communities expect."
People were advised against bathing at Exmouth after a pollution incident last year [BBC]
A separate report from the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat said South West Water's drinking water quality "remains exceptional, and consumers can be confident that their water is safe to drink".
It noted although its internal sewer flooding performance had deteriorated, "it is still performing better than the industry average".
However, it said overall environmental performance "is poor".
In a summary, the report said overall water supply interruptions "remain a significant concern, and it is one of the worst performers in the industry".
To improve the company needed to reduce interruptions and complete a transformation programme to address the root causes of its failures and "substantially improve customer interactions and overall experience", it said.
Surfers Against Sewage described the latest performance ratings as "another league of shame for water companies" but she added they were "a mere slap on the wrist that means absolutely nothing".
Head of campaigns Jo Morley said: "What is the point in these environmental performance ratings when year after year water company behaviour gets worse?"

articles.title_orig: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing
ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines said Thursday its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing.
The restrictions have raised concerns over potential revenue losses and disruptions to Mongolia’s massive mineral sector.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC, which operates Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world’s largest copper mines, said the number of truck convoys transporting copper concentrate across the Chinese border has fallen from the usual 12 to 13 per day to just around four. The restrictions affect vehicles crossing at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port, which is adjacent to Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait Border Port.
The export cuts amount to a decline of about $300 million compared to normal operating conditions and could reach $1.2 billion if restrictions continue through the end of the year, local media reported on Wednesday.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC did not confirm the reported losses in a statement to The Associated Press on Thursday.
Mongolia is a major supplier of coal and copper to China, the world’s largest consumer of both commodities.
Mongolian border officials said the slowdown was related to infrastructure and technology upgrades at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port.
Authorities in China’s Inner Mongolia region did not immediately answer questions from the AP.
In August, Chinese authorities introduced an in-vehicle facial recognition system for truck drivers crossing the border, and installation and maintenance work have affected border processing capacity, according to the Mongolian border authorities.
Mongolia’s government said the Chinese embassy in Ulaanbaatar informed it that the work, originally due to end by late September according to Mongolian news reports, may continue until the end of December.
Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said some ministers were instructed during a Cabinet meeting to visit the border crossing and meet with Chinese authorities, according to local news reports.
All transport routes on the Mongolian side remain open and the government was not aware of any political reasons behind the restrictions, said the minister of Road and Transport, Delgersaikhan Borkhuu.
Mongolia’s copper sector has become an increasingly important contributor to national export revenues. During the first nine months of 2026, copper concentrate exports reportedly reached 2 million tons.
The border crossing restrictions have also affected Mongolia’s coal exports through Gashuunsukhait, with the number of vehicles crossing falling to just over 1,000 a day from 1,300 a day, border authorities said.
Mongolia has abundant mineral resources, including coal, copper, gold, uranium and fluorspar, and its economy relies heavily on mining, which accounts for roughly a quarter of its GDP. It is particularly sensitive to disruptions to cross-border trade and fluctuations in commodity prices.
Last year, coal and copper concentrates together accounted for 82.3% of Mongolia’s merchandise exports, while 89.4% of total exports went to China. Mongolia was also China’s leading supplier of imported coking coal, accounting for approximately 51% of Chinese coking coal imports in 2025.
